explain.say: Here is a surprise: about 100 years ago, many shops in the USA said pink was for boys and blue was for girls! So colour rules are not natural; they are learned. Look at the board. It shows how gender stereotypes build up as we grow.

explain.say: See words we hear? Phrases like boys don't cry or be ladylike teach children what is expected. This learning from family, friends, school and media is called socialisation. And see fixed ideas? A 2017 study found that by age 6, many girls already thought boys were more likely to be brilliant. How does that make you feel?

faq.q: Where do gender stereotypes come from?
faq.a: Mostly from what we learn as we grow up: from clothes and toys, films and books, adverts, and the words of family and friends. This learning is called socialisation.
asks: How do children learn gender roles?

faq.q: Was pink always a girl colour?
faq.a: No. In the early 1900s some US shops and magazines said pink suited boys and blue suited girls. The pink-for-girls rule became common only from around the 1940s.
Toys marketed only to boys or only to girls can send messages about who builds, cares or explores. Many shops in the UK and elsewhere have moved to gender-neutral toy aisles.
asks: Should toys be for boys or girls?

faq.q: How do films and books shape gender ideas?
faq.a: When boys are often shown as heroes and girls as helpers, children may come to think that is how things should be. More varied stories help children imagine more possibilities.
asks: Tell me about screens and books

faq.q: At what age do children learn gender stereotypes?
faq.a: Very early. Many children know common stereotypes by age 3 to 5, and a 2017 study by Bian and colleagues found that by age 6 many girls thought boys were more likely to be really, really smart.

facts: A 1918 US trade magazine article advised pink for boys and blue for girls; the reverse became common in the mid-1900s.
Bian, Leslie and Cimpian (2017, Science) found that by age 6, girls were less likely than boys to believe their own gender was "really, really smart".
